system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2124-01-28 19:51:00 to 2124-02-02 17:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, found to be in mild diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by a viral gastroenteritis and bronchiolitis. She was treated with IV fluids and insulin, which resolved the DKA. An upper endoscopy showed mild esophagitis and gastric erythema likely from vomiting, with biopsies pending for H. pylori. She received a course of levofloxacin for bronchiolitis and was started on citalopram for anxiety and panic attacks. Her Lantus dose was reduced to 20 units at discharge to prevent hypoglycemia, and she was advised to follow up with her PCP for mental health and GI evaluation, including a possible gastric emptying study. She was discharged home in stable condition, tolerating oral intake, with instructions to monitor blood glucose and avoid narcotics.
problems: Intestinal infection due to other organism, not elsewhere classified
Diabetes with ketoacidosis, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
Acute bronchiolitis due to other infectious organisms

Discharge note 1 (2124-02-02 00:00:00): Name:  ___                Unit No:   ___
 
Admission Date:  ___              Discharge Date:   ___
 
Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: MEDICINE
 
Allergies:

Attending: ___
 
Chief Complaint:
abdominal pain

none

 
History of Present Illness:
This is a ___ year old female with a history of IDDM (Hb A1c 
11.1), anxiety who has had multiple admission for DKA and 
abdominal pain who presented to BI with abdominal pain, nausea 
and vomiting.  Patient is a poor historian.  It seems the 
patient never completely was symptoms free from her last 
admission.  She
became worse a few days ago with pain, nausea, vomiting and 
inability to take PO.  She tolerated some chicken soup but was 
unable to tolerate anything else.  She reported a crampy mid 
epigastric pain ___ in severity without radiation.  She has 
been taking her mothers narcotics for pain.  

Of note she was admitted in ___ for similar symptoms.  GI 
was consulted at that time and patient underwent an EGD which 
revealed H. Pylori.  A gastric emptying study was recommended as 
an outpatient but has not been done.  

Limited review of systems, patient does not endorse hematemesis, 
melena or BRBPR.  Nausea and emesis.
 
Past Medical History:
-Diabetes Type I: diagnosed age ___ in ___ after her first 
pregnancy. Most recent Hgb A1C 9.7 % (___), last seen at 
___ on ___  
- Stage I diabetic nephropathy  
- Anxiety/panic attacks  
- Depression  
- Esophagitis / H. Pylori ___  
- Hyperlipidemia  
- S/P MVA ___ - lower back pain since then. Per patient  
received oxycodone from her primary provider  
- ___  
- G2P1Ab1, s/p miscarriage in ___ trimester, s/p ___ 
in ___, not menstruating secondary to being on ___  
- Genital Herpes  

 
Physical Exam:
VS -  T: 99.6, BP: 140/100, HR: 96, RR: 18, O2: 96% on RA. 
Gen: Tearful, anxious, decreased attention, short answers.    
HEENT:  Conjunctiva were pink, no pallor or cyanosis of the oral
mucosa.   
CV:  S1, S2. No m/r/g. No thrills, lifts. No S3 or S4.  
Chest:  CTAB, no crackles, wheezes or rhonchi.  
Abd: Soft, Tender to palpation greatest in epigastric region
although mild tenderness diffusely. No HSM or tenderness.  No
LAD. Patient became nauseous dur ring exam.    
Ext: No c/c/e.  
Pelvic exam in ED noted to be normal
 
Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ yo woman with poorly controlled type I DM. 
She was admitted with nausea, vomiting and diarrhea as well as 
abdominal pain and was found to be 
hyperglycemic with a modest anion gap. Her hyperglycemia and 
anion gap resolved with hydration, however, she had persistent 
abdominal pain and nausea and vomiting for several days during 
her stay. She was evaluated by the GI service, who recommended a 
gastric emptying study to evaluate for gastroparesis, a stool 
test for h pylori, and a flexible sigmoidoscopy (for colitis 
seen on admission abdominal CT scan). As the patient decided she 
wanted to leave the hospital on ___, these will need to be 
arranged as an outpatient. In addition, she was evaluated by 
psychiatry as she had frequent anxiety as an inpatient and 
outbursts towards her caregivers. ___ recommended ___ 
as well as ativan tid to help with her symptoms. They also 
recommended outpatient psychiatry ___. Case management and 
social work were involved in trying to help set up her 
psychiatry ___ and to centralize her care (at ___, as 
the patient has difficulty showing up for outpatient appts. She 
also needs an outpatient case manager.

 
Discharge Medications:
1. Pantoprazole 40 mg Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) Sig: One 
(1) Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) PO once a day.  
2. Mirtazapine 15 mg Tablet Sig: 0.5 Tablet PO HS (at bedtime).
Disp:*30 Tablet(s)* Refills:*2*
3. Ezetimibe 10 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO DAILY (Daily).  

4. ___ 81 mg Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) Sig: One (1) 
Tablet, Delayed Release (E.C.) PO once a day.  
5. Insulin Glargine 100 unit/mL Cartridge Sig: Eight (8) units 
Subcutaneous at bedtime.  
6. Insulin Lispro 100 unit/mL Cartridge Sig: as directed on 
sliding scale units Subcutaneous three times a day: Please 
resume the 1:40 correction and 1:14 for insulin to carb ratio.  
7. Ativan 0.5 mg Tablet Sig: One (1) Tablet PO three times a day 
as needed for anxiety.
Disp:*50 Tablet(s)* Refills:*0*

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
PrimarY: 
nausea/vomitting/abd pain
poorly controlled DMI

 
Discharge Condition:
vital signs stable. 

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain, nausea 
and vomitting. These resolved with antiemetics. It is likely 
that you gastroparesis, which is a problem with the motility of 
your stomach, seconday to diabetes. You should have a gastric 
emptying study done as an outpatient to evaluate this. You also 
had thickening in your bowerl, which needs to be evaluated with 
a sigmoidoscopy. You will have to schedule these tomorrow. We 
wanted to keep you in the hospital to do these two studies, but 
you prefer to do them as an outpatient.

IT IS VERY IMPORTANT THAT YOU SCHEDULE NECESSARY STUDIES ON 
DISCHARGE. PLEASE FOLLOW UP WITH YOUR GI DOCTOR. 

The following changes were made to your medication regimen. 
please take all medications as prescribed: 
1. START Mirtazapine 7.5mg (that is half a pill) to be taken 
every night to help with sleep. 
2. STOP Celexa, as this did not help
3. YOU CAN TAKE ATIVAn 1 pill up to 3 times a day for anxiety. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS.

COMPARISON:  ___ and ___.

HISTORY:  Diabetes, abdominal pain and nausea and vomiting, evaluate for
obstruction.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axially acquired images through the abdomen and pelvis were
obtained.  IV contrast was administered.  Coronal and sagittal reformats were
performed.

FINDINGS:

CT ABDOMEN:  The lung bases are clear.  There is no pericardial or pleural
effusion.  The spleen, liver, gallbladder, adrenal glands are unremarkable.
The pancreas is normal in appearance.  The kidneys enhance and excrete
contrast symmetrically.  Slight striated pattern within the kidneys may be due
to phase of contrast and is stable when compared to prior exam.  The adrenal
glands are unremarkable.  Small bowel loops are normal in caliber.  There is
no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  There is no free air.

CT OF THE PELVIS:  The appendix is normal.  There is mild colonic wall
thickening involving the entire colon, sparing the cecum.  In addition, mild
perirectal soft tissue stranding is also identified.  These findings are
stable when compared to ___ and were likely present since ___.
There is no pelvic or inguinal lymphadenopathy.  The bladder and uterus are
unremarkable.

BONE WINDOWS:  There are no suspicious lytic or sclerotic lesions identified.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Colonic wall thickening which appears chronic and stable in distribution
and severity since ___.  Given stability, this less likely is
thought to represent infectious or inflammatory etiologies.

2.  Normal appendix.  No evidence of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… it’s this crampy pain in the middle of my stomach. It’s been going on for a while, but got worse a few days ago. I can’t keep anything down except a little soup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you had any fever, blood in your stool, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. I did feel a little feverish, but not sure. My stomach just hurts and I keep throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your blood sugar when you came in, and it was high. You also had a small acid buildup, which we call a modest anion gap. That’s common in uncontrolled diabetes. We’re starting IV fluids and insulin to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my sugars have been high. I’ve been stressed. I’ve been using my mom’s pain pills to help with the stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you're allergic to morphine, so we won’t use that. But we’ll manage your pain safely. We also ordered a CT scan to check your abdomen. It showed some thickening in the colon, but it looks stable and not acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? The colon thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been there a while, so it’s not an emergency. But we do need to check it further. The GI team recommends a sigmoidoscopy as an outpatient to make sure it’s not colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I was supposed to get a stomach test before, but I never went.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a gastric emptying study. That’s still important. Given your diabetes and ongoing nausea, we think you might have gastroparesis — that’s when the stomach doesn’t empty properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel full and sick all the time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And it’s common in people with long-standing diabetes. We’ll need that test to confirm. We also want a stool test for H. pylori, since you had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I don’t want to stay in the hospital long. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focused on getting your blood sugar under control and keeping you hydrated. The nausea is improving with anti-nausea meds. But you’ll need to follow up on those tests after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are better today. The acid in your blood has cleared, and your sugars are coming down with the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I still feel kind of shaky though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching that. It could be from the insulin or from not eating. We’re trying to get you to tolerate small sips. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad. I’m just so anxious. I hate being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatry team saw you yesterday. They think your anxiety is making things harder. They recommend starting mirtazapine at night for sleep and anxiety, and you can take Ativan up to three times a day as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on Celexa before. Did that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They reviewed it and think it hasn’t been effective, so we’re stopping it. Mirtazapine might help more with both sleep and appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test came back. It showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination from skin or genital area, so we don’t think you have a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’re focusing on your diabetes, stomach issues, and anxiety. Your blood pressure is a bit high too, but we’ll manage that with your regular meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You’ve been off IV fluids since this morning and tolerating small amounts of food. Your pain is less, and you’re not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you a bit longer to finish monitoring, but we understand you want to leave. The GI team wanted to do the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy here, but we can arrange them as outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather do them outside. I just can’t stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set that up. But it’s very important you schedule them soon. Gastroparesis and colon changes need to be checked properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll call. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your vitals are stable. You’ve been eating soft foods without vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole for stomach protection, ezetimibe for cholesterol, and your insulin. We’re adjusting your long-acting insulin to 8 units at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s lower than before. Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your sugars were high but now are improving. We don’t want you going too low, especially if you’re not eating well. You’ll also take half a mirtazapine pill at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one tablet up to three times a day for anxiety. But don’t take more than that. We also recommend following up with a psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need help. I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Case management is helping set up appointments at Central Clinic. It might be easier for you to go to one place for all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I get confused with all the different doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re stable, no fever, and you’ve been eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, call your GI doctor to schedule the gastric emptying study and sigmoidoscopy. They’re important to understand your stomach and colon issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call today. I mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, take your new meds as directed. Watch your blood sugar closely. If you start vomiting again or your sugars go very high, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel really anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the Ativan as needed, but also try to reach your counselor. We’ve set up a case manager to help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do better this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take care, and please follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave — are you feeling okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m feeling much better. Still a little nervous, but I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Remember, the Ativan is there if you need it. And call the clinic if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge instructions are in your packet. The key points are: schedule the GI tests, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve already called the GI office. They’re mailing me the prep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep that momentum. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your insulin again before you leave. Make sure you’re comfortable with the doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’ve got it. 8 units at night, and the fast-acting with meals based on my sugar and carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And use the sliding scale if your sugar is high. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your A1c was high at 9.7%. We know diabetes is hard to manage, especially with everything else going on. But controlling it helps prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll try harder. I don’t want to lose my kidneys or go blind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already taking steps. That’s what matters. We believe you can do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you have a ride home and someone to check on you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister’s picking me up and staying tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take it easy, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these printed instructions with you. Call the clinic Monday to confirm your appointments.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes was admitted for abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and hyperglycemia with a modest anion gap, consistent with mild diabetic ketoacidosis. Her metabolic abnormalities resolved with IV fluids and insulin therapy. Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms led to a GI consultation, which recommended outpatient evaluation for suspected gastroparesis with a gastric emptying study and assessment of chronic colonic wall thickening via flexible sigmoidoscopy. The patient declined inpatient procedures and opted for discharge. Psychiatry evaluated her for anxiety and recommended switching from citalopram to mirtazapine and using as-needed Ativan. She was discharged home with stable vital signs, improved symptoms, and a plan to follow up on pending studies and mental health care. Case management arranged centralized outpatient care to improve adherence.
